canonicalExplanation.summary: Code review asks: **is this change correct, safe, tested, maintainable, and does it meet the issue's criteria?** Read the PR description first, then the tests, then the code. Good feedback is **actionable**: it names the **location**, the **consequence**, and a **specific change or question**. Label the weight of each comment so the author can prioritise: **blocker** (must fix before merge: bugs, security, missing tests), **suggestion** (optional improvement) and **question** (you need to understand something). Personal style preferences that a linter doesn't enforce shouldn't block a correct change. Be kind: review the code, not the person.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner reviews a classmate's PR and leaves one comment: "needs work". The author has no idea what to change and asks. Meanwhile a real crash on empty input goes unnoticed. A reviewer points to an unchecked empty input, explains the resulting crash, and requests a focused boundary test rather than writing vague needs work feedback. In this lesson you'll submit prioritized review feedback and distinguish blocker, suggestion and question.

```predict
{"question": "Which comment can the author act on right away?", "options": ["\"This could be better.\"", "\"Line 14: items[0] crashes when items is empty. Can you guard it and add a test for []?\""], "answer": 1, "why": "Location + consequence + concrete request."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Remotes and synchronization**, **Pull request narrative** and **Diffs and patch review**.

sections.heading: The rule: location, consequence, request, weight
sections.body:
```text
[blocker] src/cart.js:14
  items[0].price throws TypeError when items is empty (empty cart page
  crashes). Please return 0 for [] and add a test for the empty case.

[suggestion] src/cart.js:20
  Optional: reduce() with an initial value would remove the loop.

[question] src/cart.js:31
  Why round here rather than at display time? Is it for the tax rule?
```

| Check | Ask |
|---|---|
| requirements. | does it meet the issue's acceptance criteria? |
| correctness. | edge cases: empty, zero, null, very large? |
| security. | untrusted input, secrets, permissions? |
| tests. | would a test fail if the fix were reverted? |
| maintainability. | clear names, no duplicated logic? |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Should you block a PR because you'd name a variable differently?", "answer": "No, unless it violates a project convention. Make it a suggestion. Blockers are for correctness, security, requirements and missing tests."}
```

sections.heading: Quality over quantity

includes: Review for requirements, correctness, security, tests and maintainability.
Write actionable comments labelled blocker, suggestion or question.

outcomes: Submit prioritized review feedback and distinguish blocker, suggestion and question.

examples.title: The unchecked empty input
examples.situation: A reviewer points to an unchecked empty input, explains the resulting crash, and requests a focused boundary test rather than writing vague needs work feedback.
walkthrough: **Points to an unchecked empty input:** "[blocker] cart.js:14, items[0] with items = []".
**Explains the resulting crash:** the empty cart page throws TypeError.
**Requests a focused boundary test:** "return 0 for [] and add a test", rather than vague needs work feedback; the author will fix it in one commit.
examples.result: The crash is caught before merge, and the author knows exactly what to do.

examples.title: The style war
examples.situation: A reviewer blocks a correct PR three times over brace placement and naming preferences not in the style guide.
walkthrough: If the team cares, add a formatter or linter rule instead.
Approve the correct change and leave optional suggestions.
examples.result: The fix ships, and style is settled once by tooling instead of in every review.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Review quality is measured by the number of comments, and personal style differences should block a correct change.
misconceptions.correction: Good reviews catch correctness, security, requirement and test gaps with clear, prioritised comments. Style preferences belong to tooling or to optional suggestions.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "Quality over quantity", which review protected users?

analogy.example: Reviewing is like **a building inspection**. The inspector notes "stairwell 2: missing handrail, fall risk, install before occupancy" (blocker), "consider brighter bulbs" (suggestion), and "what's this pipe for?" (question). They don't fail the building over paint colour.
limitations: Inspectors follow codes; reviewers follow the project's standards.
Questions are welcome: they often reveal hidden problems.

nearTransfer.prompt: Rewrite these review comments to be actionable and labelled: "meh", "why??", "this is wrong", "I'd do it differently".
scaffold: Invent a plausible location and consequence.

farTransfer.prompt: Review a partner's small PR (or a provided diff). Produce at least one blocker, suggestion and question if warranted, each with location, consequence and request, then discuss with the author and record what changed.

remediation.explanation: For every comment ask: **where, so what, what should change, and how important is it?** If you can't say "so what", it's probably a preference.

recap.summary: To submit prioritised review feedback, read the description and tests first, check requirements, correctness, security and maintainability, and write comments that give location, consequence and a concrete request, labelled blocker, suggestion or question, without blocking on personal style.
